doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
title: Singing on the WWVA amateur hour and Uncle John
summary: As a child he auditioned and sang on WWVA radio, and his dancer uncle John noticed him improvising on a song.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And there was a row of kids with their mothers.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. There was a skinny little red-haired girl, she might have had freckles even, she was singing and she had a violin you know. And it came her turn, and in the 30s it was [scats]. Benny Goodman made a record of it, it was a pop tune [scats].
You never heard of it, huh?

But it’s on a discography, Benny made a record and others. Bad thing. And so this little girl [screeches scats] well you could fall on the floor, even when I was a kid I said, “boy that’s pretty terrible,” scratching I mean. So we all did the thing, and I made the auditions. And I sang on the radio twice, can you imagine? Now I don’t remember whether it was the Amateur Hour program or whether they put the winning amateurs on some bigger program. But the strange thing was — what did I sing and how did I pick it? I haven’t the vaguest. [sings] “There’s a goldmine in the sky far away/we will find it you and I some sweet day.” Nick Kenny, you ever hear of Nick Kenny?

Nick Kenny, he was a columnist in the news or something and he wrote lyrics for songs. And this was one of his, it’s a sentimental thing, goldmine — and the other one was “There’s a goldmine in the sky far away.” So I sang them.

Somebody played. Oh yeah, they had a piano player I guess. There was accompaniment. I wasn’t alone. But when I think of it I was just seven or eight. And that was sort of bizarre. And I very rarely run through this in my mind, and connecting it to later things, you know. So it started then. And then I kept singing and then my parents left Ohio — not professionally or anything, just amateur. My father had — I had only one uncle, my uncle John. And my father was sort of on the square side and John was the direct opposite, a hellion. Women loved him. Very handsome. He looked like Clark Gable sort of. And he was with a Hungarian dance company. And he sang and danced professionally. And the first time he heard me sing “Pennies From Heaven” he comes up to me and he says you know that thing you sang in there? That’s not in the song. I said well I just sort of like that.
